content: The provision of water supply involves either self-provision or the involvement of third parties to deliver water of varying qualities to different users. This discussion primarily focuses on public water supply, with industrial self-supply and irrigation addressed separately. Global Access to Water Supply As of 2004, approximately 3.5 billion people globally (54% of the population) had access to piped water through household connections. An additional 1.3 billion people (20%) accessed safe water through alternative means, such as standpipes, water kiosks, protected springs, and wells. However, over 1 billion people (16%) lacked access to safe water, relying on unprotected sources like wells, springs, canals, lakes, or rivers. Water and Public Health Adequate water quantity and quality are critical for public health and hygiene. Waterborne diseases are a leading cause of illness and death in lowand middle-income countries. Annually, around 900 million people suffer from water-related diarrheal diseases, with approximately 2 million fatalities. Diarrhea and intestinal worm infestations account for at least 17% of the total disease burden in many developing nations. Common waterborne diseases include diarrhea, typhoid, and cholera. Trachoma, an infectious eye disease leading to blindness, is also linked to inadequate water supply, poor sanitation, and improper waste management. In cases of suspected or confirmed pathogen contamination, authorities may issue boil water advisories to mitigate risks. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines basic water access as 20 liters per person per day, which is associated with significant health concerns, while optimal access is 100 liters per person per day, linked to minimal health concerns. Technical Overview of Water Supply Water supply systems source water from groundwater (aquifers), surface water (lakes and rivers), conservation efforts, or desalination of seawater. The water is typically treated through purification, disinfection (commonly chlorination), and sometimes fluoridation. Treated water is then distributed via gravity or pumping to reservoirs, which may be elevated (e.g., water towers) or ground-based. After use, wastewater is discharged into sewer systems, treated at wastewater plants, and either released into natural water bodies or reused for purposes like irrigation or industrial applications. Service Quality Despite access to piped water, many individuals, particularly in developing countries, experience poor service quality. Continuity of Supply In developed countries, continuous water supply is standard. However, in many developing nations, water is often available only intermittently, sometimes for a few hours daily or a few days weekly. Approximately half of the population in developing countries receives water on an intermittent basis. Water Quality Drinking water quality is assessed based on microbiological and physicochemical parameters. Public water systems must disinfect water, traditionally using chlorination or, more recently, ultraviolet light. Surface water often requires additional treatment. Comparing Utility Performance Benchmarking the performance of water and sanitation utilities is essential due to the natural monopoly of the sector. Benchmarking simulates competition, sets improvement targets, and encourages lagging utilities to adopt best practices. Institutional Responsibility and Governance Water supply responsibilities are divided between policy/regulatory institutions and service providers. Policy and Regulation Policies and regulations are typically established by government ministries or agencies. For example, in the US, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) oversees water and sanitation policies. Regulatory agencies, often autonomous, are tasked with tariff approvals, performance monitoring, and consumer complaint resolution. However, their independence varies across countries. Service Provision Service providers differ in geographical coverage, sectoral responsibilities, ownership, and governance. Some utilities serve single municipalities, while others operate regionally or nationally. Utilities may focus solely on water supply or also manage sewerage, wastewater treatment, and even electricity distribution. Ownership structures include public, private, mixed, or cooperative models. Governance arrangements influence financial autonomy, service quality, and the ability to recover costs through tariffs. Tariffs Most water providers charge tariffs to recover costs. Globally, the average water tariff is $0.53 per cubic meter, with higher rates in developed countries ($1.04) compared to developing nations ($0.11). However, few utilities fully recover their costs, relying on subsidies or cross-subsidies. Tariff structures vary, with some based on usage (metered) and others fixed. In developing countries, cross-subsidies often aim to make water affordable for low-income users but may inadvertently benefit wealthier segments. Metering Water metering promotes conservation, delays system expansion, identifies distribution losses, and enables fair cost allocation. Metering is common in developed countries but less so in developing nations, where about half of urban systems are metered. Meter readings can be collected manually, electronically, or via automated systems. Costs and Financing Water supply costs are predominantly fixed (capital and personnel), with variable costs (energy and chemicals) playing a smaller role. In developed countries, urban water supply costs range from $1-2 per cubic meter, with similar costs for sanitation. These costs are lower in developing nations. Financing comes from tariffs, subsidies, and debt, including loans from commercial banks, international financial institutions, and bonds. History of Water Supply Water supply systems have evolved over centuries. Ancient Rome featured aqueducts and indoor plumbing. Modern water purification methods, such as chlorination, were developed in the early 20th century, revolutionizing public health and water safety.
